prompt: A page uses <div class="nav"> for its navigation links instead of <nav>. What is the concrete, measurable consequence of this choice?
choices: The links will not be clickable in most browsers
The CSS will fail to apply because div cannot be styled the same way
Screen readers lose the ability to jump to it as a landmark, and search engines lose a structural signal for what that content is
Nothing changes; div and nav are functionally identical in every way

prompt: In mobile-first responsive CSS, what do the base (non-media-query) rules target, and what kind of media query is then added to scale up?
choices: Base rules target the widest desktop layout; max-width queries strip features away for smaller screens
Base rules target the narrowest mobile layout; min-width queries progressively add complexity for larger screens
Base rules target print layout; screen queries are added for all digital displays
There is no base rule in mobile-first; every rule lives inside a media query

prompt: A divider image is purely decorative and conveys no content. What is the correct way to handle its alt text?
choices: Omit the alt attribute entirely so screen readers skip the image
Use alt="decorative image" so the purpose is clear
Use alt="" (present but empty) so screen readers skip announcing it

prompt: Gray text at #999999 on a white background measures a contrast ratio of about 2.85:1. Per WCAG 2.1 Level AA for normal-size text, what does this mean?
choices: It passes, since AA only requires 2:1 for body text
It fails, since AA requires at least 4.5:1 for normal-size text
It passes AAA but fails the lower AA standard, which is a contradiction
